name: Costa Rica
summary: Costa Rica has freedom of testation. A will must, however, secure maintenance (alimentos) for young or disabled children, the spouse and parents who need it (Civil Code art. 595); the legítima of the pre-1888 code no longer exists. Trusts exist by statute (fideicomiso), foundations are non-profit, and Costa Rica is not in the Hague Trusts Convention.
family_claims: The testator must secure maintenance for children until adulthood (for life if disabled), and for parents and a spouse while they need it (Código Civil art. 595); if the will does not, heirs take only what is left after that maintenance. Family Code (Ley 5476) gives the surviving spouse further rights.
foreign_law_note: Not sourced. No Costa Rican conflict rule for succession and no choice of law was found.
trust_note: The fideicomiso is regulated in the Código de Comercio (arts. 633 ff.), which I did not read here; common-law trusts are not part of the law and foreign trusts' treatment was not sourced. Foundations: Ley de Fundaciones (Ley 5338 of 1973) allows foundations for non-profit purposes; whether a family foundation is possible was not verified. Not in the Hague Trusts Convention.
open_questions: Code of Commerce trust articles and Ley 5338 (foundations) were not read; both entries are 'limited' pending checks.
Whether art. 595 should be read as a compulsory share is debated in the literature (see source); treated here as a maintenance duty.
Conflict rule for succession and treatment of foreign heirs were not sourced.
